title: The Hyatt Regency Skywalk Disaster
summary: The hosts examine the July 1981 Hyatt Regency Skywalk collapse in Kansas City, Missouri, during a weekend tea dance in the atrium, which killed 114 people and injured more than 200. They describe the collapse of the second- and fourth-floor walkways, the rescue and triage efforts, the flooding from a burst sprinkler pipe, and the cause: a rushed design change that replaced one continuous rod with two offset rod sets, approved by phone and stamped without calculations by the fabricator, architect Daniel Duncan, and engineer of record Jack Gillham. They cover the Missouri Board of Professional Engineers tribunal, the more than 130 lawsuits and settlements (mostly paid by Hallmark), the city's long recovery, the 2008 memorial, and changes in engineering oversight and first responder PTSD care. The episode closes with listener mail about a Gollum/Smeagol voice mix-up.
topics: Missouri Board of Professional Engineers tribunal
largest structural disaster in American history

segments.title: Opening and content warning
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode on the Hyatt Regency tragedy in Kansas City and warn that some details are gruesome.

segments.title: Hotel background and tea dance
segments.summary: The hotel, part of Hallmark's Crown Center complex, opened in July 1980. On a Friday night in July 1981, around a thousand to two thousand people were in the atrium for a popular weekend tea dance when the walkways began to fall.

segments.title: The walkway collapse and immediate aftermath
segments.summary: The second- and fourth-floor skywalks fell onto the crowd, with the fourth landing on the second. Witnesses described survivors pinned, bystanders rushing to help, and fast responses from fire, police and nearby hospitals.

segments.title: Death toll and survivor stories
segments.summary: The death toll was 114, with more than 200 injured. The hosts describe individual survivors and victims, including Mark Williams, Lynn Vander Hayden and Oscar Grimm.

segments.title: Amputations, first responder trauma, and flooding
segments.summary: Rescuers amputated limbs on scene to free victims. Many first responders later suffered PTSD, suicides and substance abuse, which led to PTSD therapy changes. Water from a burst sprinkler pipe threatened trapped people until a fire chief had the front doors bulldozed.

segments.title: Recovery equipment and public mood
segments.summary: Companies donated forklifts and cranes, and a large crane was eventually needed. The public wanted to know who was to blame.

segments.title: Skywalk design and the fatal change
segments.summary: The original design used one continuous threaded rod through both floors. The change to two rod sets, approved by phone, doubled the load on the fourth-floor connection. Walkways were about 120 feet long, with box beams and hanging rods.

segments.title: Load capacity, code, and investigation
segments.summary: The National Bureau of Standards found the connection capacity was 81 kilonewtons versus a load of about 95, and the code required about 181. Welds and bolts failed. The fabricator, architect Daniel Duncan and engineer Jack Gillham approved the change without calculations.

segments.title: Lack of oversight and warning signs
segments.summary: Workers had seen beams bending during construction, and an earlier roof collapse had occurred during the build. The hosts argue no one spoke up.

segments.title: Negligence tribunal and late-1970s construction climate
segments.summary: The Missouri Board of Professional Engineers found Gillham grossly negligent. The hosts link the era to other failures, including Kemper Arena, Hartford Civic Center and Champlain Towers.
topics: Missouri Board of Professional Engineers tribunal

segments.title: Lawsuits and settlements
segments.summary: There were more than 130 lawsuits, with settlements totaling about $140 million, mostly paid by Hallmark. Individual settlements ranged from $500 to $1,000 per person, with a widow receiving $600,000.

segments.title: Hallmark, the city, and the memorial
segments.summary: The Kansas City Star and Times pursued reporting despite community pushback. The city was shaken for years, and a memorial was built in 2008 with $25,000 from Hallmark. The hosts describe the skywalk remaining with column supports and changes to ASCE guidance.

segments.title: Closing reflections
segments.summary: The hosts reflect that one decision caused the collapse and say they hope to visit Kansas City one day.

segments.title: Listener mail: Smeagol vs. Smiegel
segments.summary: A listener points out that Chuck has been calling Josh's Gollum voice 'Smiegel' rather than Smeagol, and that the Megal in the toll house voice is funnier as a result.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and give the email address and show credits.
